definitions.definition: The Lord, Śiva: one, eternally free (anādimukta), omniscient and omnipotent, the efficient cause who by his single power performs the five acts for the souls' release; distinct from souls and bonds.
Pati (Tamil pati, iṟai): the Lord who is one with, other than and together with souls; the Real (cat).
The bound soul: eternal, countless, by nature a conscious knower and agent (cit), all-pervading, whose powers are covered by beginningless mala; 'tethered animal' of the Lord.
The soul (Tamil uyir, āṉmā, pacu): sadasat, knowing only when made to know, taking on the nature of what it is joined with.
The bonds: āṇava mala, karma and māyā (with Śiva's concealing power counted as a bond, and bindu for souls in the pure worlds); eternal realities, not appearances.
Pācam: the three (or five) malas that bind the soul; eternal, their power quelled in release.
In the narrow sense āṇava mala; in the wide sense any of the bonds. A real substance (dravya), not ignorance.
Malam: impurity; 'the three malas' (mummalam) are āṇavam, kaṉmam and māyai.
The innate (sahaja) impurity of the soul, one in substance with countless powers, beginningless, covering its powers of knowing and acting; it ripens and is removed by Śiva's power in initiation.
Āṇavam, the 'dark mala' (iruḷ mala) which hides even itself; never destroyed, only rendered powerless by grace.
The soul's beginningless stream of good and bad deeds (dharma and adharma) that determines birth, lifespan and experience; distributed by the Lord.
Kaṉmam / iruviṉai: the two deeds, good and bad, both binding.
The bond of māyā: the body, instruments, worlds and objects given to the soul from māyā, which both bind and help it by awakening its powers partly.
One, eternal, insentient, real substance: the material cause of the impure universe (and, as bindu or mahāmāyā, of the pure). Not illusion.

equivalents.note: māyā as material cause vs māyā as bond

definitions.definition: Māyēyam: the products of māyā (bodies, organs, worlds, objects), counted as the fourth of the five malas.
Śiva's concealing power (rodha-śakti), called a bond by figure because it impels the bonds until the soul is ripe.
Tirōtāyi / tirōtam: fifth of the five malas; 'na' of the five letters.
Pure māyā (śuddha-māyā, mahāmāyā, kuṭilā): the pure material cause of the pure universe, of the bodies of pure beings and of sound; distinct from Śiva, who does not change.
Another name of bindu, the pure material cause.
A soul bound by all three bonds — mala, karma and māyā — living in the worlds of māyā.
A soul bound by mala and karma, whose māyic body is dissolved in the cosmic dissolution.
A soul bound by mala alone, free of karma and māyā; the highest of these are raised by Śiva to offices as mantras, mantra-lords and Vidyeśvaras.
A principle or level of reality in the ascending scale of 36 from earth to Śiva; the lower 31 (or so) are products of māyā, the pure five of bindu.
Tattuvam: 36 tattvas (24 ātma, 7 vidyā, 5 śiva), elaborated to 96 in the Tamil lists.
The 'sheaths' from māyā — kalā (limited agency), vidyā (limited knowledge), rāga (attachment), kāla (time) and niyati (restriction) — which partly awaken and limit the soul for experience.
Cat-acat: the soul's nature as neither the Real (Śiva) nor the unreal (the perishing world) but able to know and join both.
'Free from beginningless time': Śiva, never bound, distinguished from liberated souls who were once bound.
The state of the liberated soul: a 'Śiva', equal to Śiva in omniscience and omnipotence, its innate powers manifest; numerically distinct from Śiva and not an agent of the cosmic acts.
The efficient cause: Śiva alone, who does not change by causing.
The material cause of the world: māyā (and bindu for the pure universe) — never Śiva.
The auxiliary or instrumental cause: Śiva's single power (śakti).
The descent of Śiva's power on a soul whose mala has ripened, qualifying it for initiation.
Catti nipātam, in four grades matched to the four pādas.
The ripening of āṇava mala, whose powers turn away until it is ready to be removed.
Malaparipākam, the ripening that accompanies the balance of deeds and precedes grace.
The first initiation, making one a samayin, entitled to the rules (samaya) and to hear the scriptures.
The 'special' initiation qualifying the initiate for the daily worship of Śiva (details vary among manuals).
The liberating initiation: the guru, as Śiva, purifies the six paths and burns the disciple's bonds; liberation follows at death, prārabdha continuing till then.
Consecration of an initiate as ācārya, entitled to initiate others and teach.
Conduct: the first of the four pādas (and a section of each Āgama) — rules of life and service.
Cariyai: temple service — cleaning, lamps, garlands, singing — the servant's path (dāsa-mārga), leading to sālokya.
Kiriyai: ritual worship of Śiva in the liṅga and image, the son's path (satputra-mārga), leading to sāmīpya.
Yōkam: inner worship and meditation on Śiva (the eightfold or sixfold yoga), the friend's path (sakhā-mārga), leading to sārūpya.
Civañāṉam: knowledge of Śiva given by grace through the guru — hearing, reflection, clarity, abiding — the true path (san-mārga), leading to sāyujya.
Niṭṭai: abiding in Śiva, the fourth step of jñāna after hearing, reflection and clarity.
Patamutti: the 'liberations in a station' — sālokya, sāmīpya, sārūpya — reached by caryā, kriyā and yoga; not final.
Paramutti: final release, sāyujya, inseparable union with Śiva reached by jñāna.
Tacakāriyam: the ten acts — form, sight and purification of tattvas, of the soul and of Śiva, then Śiva-yoga and Śiva-bhoga.

The eight Lords of Knowledge (Ananta, Sūkṣma, Śivottama, Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, Śrīkaṇṭha, Śikhaṇḍin), liberated souls in office in the pure universe who act for Śiva; Ananta governs the impure creation.
State of the soul: waking, dream, deep sleep, the fourth and beyond the fourth.
Avattai: the soul's states; also the three great conditions kēvalam (isolation with āṇava), cakalam (embodied) and cuttam (purified).
Kēvalam: the soul's condition before embodiment, alone with āṇava, knowing nothing.
Cakalam: the embodied condition with the three malas and the instruments of māyā.
Cuttam: the purified condition in which the soul, by grace, turns to Śiva.
Worship of Śiva for oneself, obligatory daily for the initiate.
Temple worship for others, performed by Ādiśaiva priests consecrated for it.
The hereditary Śaiva priests (Śivācāryas, gurukkaḷ) of South Indian temples, entitled to parārtha worship.
The five letters na-ma-śi-vā-ya (Tamil namaccivāya): concealment, mala, Śiva, grace, soul; gross form 'namaḥ śivāya', subtle 'śivāya namaḥ'.
Namaccivāya: the devotee's refuge in every danger.
Tirunīṟu, the sacred ash: mantra, medicine and the mark of Śiva's devotee.
Śiva's five acts: emission, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, grace.
Aintoḻil: paṭaittal, kāttal, aḻittal, maṟaittal, aruḷal — enacted in Naṭarāja's dance.
Turīyātītam: the fifth state beyond the fourth, in the Siddhānta account of the five avasthās.
Living in Śiva's world; fruit of caryā.
Nearness to Śiva; fruit of kriyā.
Having Śiva's form; fruit of yoga.
Inseparable union with Śiva; fruit of jñāna; the only final release.
The two deeds, good (puṇṇiyam) and bad (pāvam), both binding the soul to birth — 'golden and iron fetters'.
In the Kuṟaḷ (v. 5) the two deeds 'born of darkness' do not cling to those who praise the Lord.

The 'equality of the two deeds': the state in which the soul's good and bad karma balance, so that it turns with equal indifference from both, a precondition, with the ripening of mala, of the descent of grace.

cross_language.note: the Sanskrit Āgamic term, with a debated sense

equivalents.note: Tamil usage stresses the soul's equanimity toward both deeds; the Sanskrit term the timing of śaktipāta

definitions.definition: Grace: Śiva's own power (aruḷ-catti) acting toward the soul; ever present, it removes the power of mala and comes as the guru.
The Lord's grace that saves the devotee from every danger and cuts births.
In the Kuṟaḷ, aruḷ is compassion for all living beings (chapter 25, Aruḷuṭaimai).

equivalents.note: aruḷ is also Śiva's power itself

definitions.definition: Love for Śiva, which is itself Śiva (Tirumantiram 270).
In the Kuṟaḷ (ch. 8), love that makes one belong to others; without it the body is bone wrapped in skin.

equivalents.note: aṉpu is love in general as well as devotion

definitions.definition: Śiva as the auspicious absolute (neuter), identified with love in Tirumantiram 270.
The true or perfect reality — the Real, Śiva; in the Kuṟaḷ the reality to be seen for birth to end.
'Those at the feet': Śiva's devotees, to be served and revered as Śiva himself.
The freed soul should join the true devotees (meyyaṭiyār) and revere their garb as Śiva.
Service to Śiva and his devotees; the Nāyaṉmārs are 'toṇṭar', servants.
A hymn of (usually) ten or eleven verses, the unit of the Tēvāram, the last verse often naming the poet and promising fruit.
A melodic mode of old Tamil music to which each Tēvāram patikam is set; some two dozen are used in the Tēvāram.
Temple singers who sing the Tirumuṟai in their paṇs during worship.
'Leader, master': title of the sixty-three canonized Śaiva saints (plural Nāyaṉmār).
The four 'teachers of the religion': Appar, Campantar, Cuntarar and Māṇikkavācakar.
The teachers of the lineage: the inner line (Nandi, Sanatkumāra, Satyajñānadarśin, Parañcōti) and the outer line (Meykaṇṭār, Aruṇanti, Maṟaiñāṉa Campantar, Umāpati).
The servant's path, corresponding to caryā and exemplified by Appar.
The good son's path, corresponding to kriyā and exemplified by Campantar.
The friend's path, corresponding to yoga and exemplified by Cuntarar.
The true path of knowledge, corresponding to jñāna and exemplified by Māṇikkavācakar.
A Tamil Śaiva monastic house (maṭha) headed by a paṇṭāra-caṉṉiti, e.g. Tiruvāvaṭuturai and Dharmapuram, custodians of the Meykaṇṭa tradition and of temples.
The dance of bliss of Naṭarāja at Chidambaram, enacting the five acts.
'The space of consciousness': Chidambaram (Tillai), where Śiva dances in the 'small hall' (ciṟṟampalam); also the heart-space.

The eight qualities of the Lord (Kuṟaḷ 9's 'eṇkuṇattāṉ'), glossed by Parimēlaḻakar from the Śaiva Āgamas: self-dependence, pure body, natural understanding, omniscience, natural freedom from bonds, boundless grace, infinite power, boundless bliss.
Read by Jain interpreters of the Kuṟaḷ as the eight qualities of a liberated Siddha (reported here from the dispute; U34 may refine).
Virtue, righteousness; first of the Kuṟaḷ's three books; 'being spotless in mind is the whole of aṟam' (Kuṟaḷ 34).

equivalents.note: aṟam centres on inner purity and non-harm; dharma includes ritual duty

definitions.definition: Wealth, polity, the things of life; the Kuṟaḷ's second book (70 chapters).
Love and its joy; the Kuṟaḷ's third book (25 chapters), in the akam tradition of love poetry.
Release, liberation — the fourth aim, not a separate book in the Kuṟaḷ but implied in its chapters on renunciation and truth.
Non-killing: 'sharing food and protecting all life is the foremost precept' (Kuṟaḷ ch. 33).
Taught among the virtues of the first tantra of the Tirumantiram.
Refusing meat (Kuṟaḷ ch. 26): better than a thousand sacrifices.
Taught in the Tirumantiram's first tantra.
Truthfulness: speech that harms no one (Kuṟaḷ ch. 30).

equivalents.note: defined by the Kuṟaḷ by its harmlessness

definitions.definition: Austerity: bearing pain and not harming others (Kuṟaḷ ch. 27).
Renunciation (Kuṟaḷ ch. 35): cutting 'I' and 'mine'.
Realization of the truth (Kuṟaḷ ch. 36).
The uprooting of desire (Kuṟaḷ ch. 37), desire being the seed of all births.
Fate, the ordained outcome of former deeds (Kuṟaḷ ch. 38), mightier than any device.
Pati, the one Lord, eternally free; the efficient cause; not the material of the world; the guru of all.
Śiva's single, conscious power, the instrument (not the material) of his acts; called grace (aruḷ) when it frees, concealment when it drives the bonds.
The state of the soul freed by grace while the body, sustained by prārabdha, continues; such a one lives among devotees and acts as Śiva's servant.
